## Financial Derivatives

:::{.definition data-title="Financial Derivative"}
A **financial derivative** is a financial instrument whose value is derived
from some underlying asset, index, or rate.
:::

Think of a derivative as a **contract** between two parties that specifies the
terms of a financial transaction based on the performance of the underlying
asset. A contract typically specifies

- the **underlying** asset, index or rate,
- the **maturity** $T$, the date at which the contract is settled,
- the **strike** price $K$, a price fixed in advance in the contract.

The party that buys the contract is said to hold a **long** position and the
party that sells it holds a **short** position. Because the value of the
contract depends on the future price of the underlying, which is uncertain, a
derivative is also called a **contingent claim**.

Derivatives are used for

- **hedging**: reducing an existing risk, such as locking in a future price,
- **speculation**: taking a view on the price of the underlying,
- **leverage**: gaining large exposure to the underlying for a small outlay.

## Types of Derivatives

### Forwards

:::{.definition data-title="Forward Contract"}
A **forward contract** is a customized agreement between two parties to buy or
sell an asset at a specified price $K$ on a future date $T$. Forwards are
traded over-the-counter (OTC) and are not standardized.
:::

The holder of a long forward must buy the asset at time $T$ for $K$, so the
payoff is $S_T - K$. No money changes hands at the start, so $K$ is chosen to
make the contract worth zero at time $0$. For an asset that pays no income and
a constant interest rate $r$, no arbitrage forces
$$
K = S_0 e^{rT},
$$
since one can replicate the forward by buying the asset today with borrowed
money. See [[risk-neutral-pricing]].

### Futures

:::{.definition data-title="Futures Contract"}
A **futures contract** is a standardized agreement to buy or sell an asset at
a predetermined price on a specified future date. Futures are traded on
organized exchanges and are subject to daily settlement.
:::

Daily settlement (**marking to market**) means that gains and losses are
paid each day through a margin account held with the exchange's
clearinghouse, which removes most counterparty risk. With a constant interest
rate the futures price and the forward price of a contract coincide.

### Options

:::{.definition data-title="Option"}
An **option** is a contract that gives the holder the right, but not the
obligation, to buy (**call option**) or sell (**put option**) an asset at a
specified price (the strike price $K$) on or before a specified date (the
expiration date $T$).
:::

The buyer pays the seller an up-front amount called the **premium**. A
**European** option can only be exercised at the expiration date, while an
**American** option can be exercised at any time before it. See [[option-pricing]].

### Swaps

:::{.definition data-title="Swap"}
A **swap** is a derivative contract in which two parties agree to exchange
cash flows or other financial instruments over a specified period. Common
types of swaps include interest rate swaps and currency swaps.
:::

In a **fixed-for-floating interest rate swap**, one party pays a fixed rate $K$
on a notional amount $N$ while the other pays a floating rate (such as SOFR,
which has replaced LIBOR) at regular dates. At each date the fixed payer
receives $N\,(L - K)\,\Delta$, where $L$ is the floating rate and $\Delta$ the
length of the period. See [[interest-rates]].

## Payoff Functions

:::{.definition data-title="Payoff"}
The **payoff** of a derivative is the amount the holder receives at maturity.
:::

We model the price of the underlying by a
[[stochastic-processes|stochastic process]] $(S_t)$, so the payoff is a random
variable. For a payoff that depends only on the final price we write
$h(S_T)$, and for a payoff that depends on the whole path we write
$h(S_{[0,T]})$. The payoffs of the contracts above are

| Contract | Payoff $h(S_T)$ |
| - | - |
| Long forward | $S_T - K$ |
| Short forward | $K - S_T$ |
| Call option | $(S_T - K)^+ = \max(S_T - K, 0)$ |
| Put option | $(K - S_T)^+ = \max(K - S_T, 0)$ |

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

source("../assets/payoff-plots.R")

K <- 100
payoff_carousel("carousel-payoffs", list(
  payoff_slide("Long call",
    "Buy a call with strike \\(K\\): \\((S_T - K)^+\\).",
    function(s) pmax(s - K, 0), K, "K"),
  payoff_slide("Short call",
    "Sell a call with strike \\(K\\): \\(-(S_T - K)^+\\).",
    function(s) -pmax(s - K, 0), K, "K"),
  payoff_slide("Long put",
    "Buy a put with strike \\(K\\): \\((K - S_T)^+\\).",
    function(s) pmax(K - s, 0), K, "K"),
  payoff_slide("Short put",
    "Sell a put with strike \\(K\\): \\(-(K - S_T)^+\\).",
    function(s) -pmax(K - s, 0), K, "K"),
  payoff_slide("Long forward",
    "Agree to buy at \\(K\\): \\(S_T - K\\).",
    function(s) s - K, K, "K"),
  payoff_slide("Short forward",
    "Agree to sell at \\(K\\): \\(K - S_T\\).",
    function(s) K - s, K, "K")
))
```

Payoffs that depend on the path of the underlying are called
**path-dependent**. Examples of these **exotic options** are

- **Asian options**, which depend on the average price,
  $h = \left(\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T S_t\,dt - K\right)^+$,
- **barrier options**, which depend on whether the price crosses a barrier.
  See [[barrier-options]],
- **lookback options**, which depend on the maximum or minimum price.

## Option Spreads and Combinations

Options can be combined to build payoffs that no single option provides. A
**spread** combines options of the same type (all calls or all puts) with
different strikes or maturities, and a **combination** mixes calls and puts.
The diagrams show the payoff at maturity. The profit is the payoff minus the
net premium paid to set up the position.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

source("../assets/payoff-plots.R")

pos <- function(x) pmax(x, 0)
payoff_carousel("carousel-spreads", list(
  payoff_slide("Bull call spread",
    paste("Long a call at \\(K_1\\), short a call at \\(K_2 > K_1\\):",
          "\\((S_T - K_1)^+ - (S_T - K_2)^+\\)."),
    function(s) pos(s - 90) - pos(s - 110), c(90, 110), c("K1", "K2")),
  payoff_slide("Bear put spread",
    paste("Long a put at \\(K_2\\), short a put at \\(K_1 < K_2\\):",
          "\\((K_2 - S_T)^+ - (K_1 - S_T)^+\\)."),
    function(s) pos(110 - s) - pos(90 - s), c(90, 110), c("K1", "K2")),
  payoff_slide("Bull put spread",
    paste("Long a put at \\(K_1\\), short a put at \\(K_2 > K_1\\):",
          "\\((K_1 - S_T)^+ - (K_2 - S_T)^+\\)."),
    function(s) pos(90 - s) - pos(110 - s), c(90, 110), c("K1", "K2")),
  payoff_slide("Bear call spread",
    paste("Short a call at \\(K_1\\), long a call at \\(K_2 > K_1\\):",
          "\\(-(S_T - K_1)^+ + (S_T - K_2)^+\\)."),
    function(s) -pos(s - 90) + pos(s - 110), c(90, 110), c("K1", "K2")),
  payoff_slide("Long straddle",
    "Long a call and a put at \\(K\\): \\(|S_T - K|\\).",
    function(s) abs(s - 100), 100, "K"),
  payoff_slide("Long strangle",
    paste("Long a put at \\(K_1\\) and a call at \\(K_2 > K_1\\):",
          "\\((K_1 - S_T)^+ + (S_T - K_2)^+\\)."),
    function(s) pos(90 - s) + pos(s - 110), c(90, 110), c("K1", "K2")),
  payoff_slide("Long butterfly",
    paste("Long calls at \\(K_1\\) and \\(K_3\\), short two calls at",
          "\\(K_2 = (K_1 + K_3)/2\\)."),
    function(s) pos(s - 80) - 2 * pos(s - 100) + pos(s - 120),
    c(80, 100, 120), c("K1", "K2", "K3")),
  payoff_slide("Iron condor",
    paste("Long a put at \\(K_1\\), short a put at \\(K_2\\), short a call",
          "at \\(K_3\\), long a call at \\(K_4\\)."),
    function(s) pos(80 - s) - pos(90 - s) - pos(s - 110) + pos(s - 120),
    c(80, 90, 110, 120), c("K1", "K2", "K3", "K4"))
))
```

### Vertical Spreads

A **vertical spread** holds a long and a short option of the same type and
maturity at two strikes $K_1 < K_2$. The payoff is bounded, so the spread
limits both the cost and the possible gain compared with a single option.

- A **bull spread** profits when the underlying rises. It can be built from
  calls (the **bull call spread**, $(S_T - K_1)^+ - (S_T - K_2)^+$) or from
  puts (the **bull put spread**).
- A **bear spread** profits when the underlying falls. It can be built from
  puts (the **bear put spread**) or from calls (the **bear call spread**).

### Straddles and Strangles

A **straddle** holds a call and a put with the same strike, and a
**strangle** holds an out-of-the-money put and call with different strikes.
Both gain when the underlying moves far in either direction, so they are bets
on large price moves (high volatility) rather than on direction.

### Butterfly and Condor

A **butterfly** with strikes $K_1 < K_2 < K_3$ and $K_2 = (K_1 + K_3)/2$ has
payoff

$$
(S_T - K_1)^+ - 2(S_T - K_2)^+ + (S_T - K_3)^+,
$$

a tent that peaks at $K_2$ with height $K_2 - K_1$. It profits when the
underlying ends close to $K_2$. The **iron condor** earns a premium and loses
a limited amount if the underlying moves outside $[K_1, K_4]$.

As the spacing between the strikes shrinks, the cost of a butterfly
approaches a second difference of call prices in the strike. This is the
idea behind the [[breeden-litzenberger-formula]], and more generally the
[[carr-madan-formula]] writes any European payoff as a combination of calls
and puts across all strikes.

## Pricing

The payoff tells us what the holder receives, but not what the contract is
worth today. The principle of no arbitrage determines the fair price. Under
the [[risk-neutral-pricing|risk-neutral measure]] $\mathbb{Q}$ with a constant
interest rate $r$, the price at time $0$ is the discounted expected payoff
$$
e^{-rT}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[h(S_T)].
$$
This is developed in [[option-pricing]].
